portions of Russia has been of most heart.
rending nature. In two provinces, thous-
ands have been stricken with diptheria.
and so great is the scarcity of food that in
some instances, children have been sold to
obtain the necessaries of life. Il seems
almost impossible to believe that sach a
state Of affairs can exist. but unfortunately
it is only too true. In some of the villages
in the stricken district whole families have
died. and their remains left, from sheer
necessity, until thoroughly decomposed.
there being none left to bury the dead.
The ravages of the yellow fever at Gren-
ada, Miss, horrible enough in its details,
bears no comparison to the famine and
disease stricken provinces of Russia.

were tardy, as usual, when 10 o'clock
arrived, the hour to which the Convention
adjourned. Very few were in their

organ, apparently being more appropriate
for Fourth of July enthusiasm.

yesterday were cheered as they entered.

At 10 o'clock the Chairman called the
Convention to order and introduced
Rev. Charles W. Taylor, of Covington,
Ky., who offered prayer.

pensed with.

offered the following resolution:

the war with Mexico, and the widows, or
orphans and the children of the soldiers de-
ceased are entitled to the grateful recognition
of the people of the United States,
and Congress ought to cause them to be
placed on the pension roll on the same
footing with the soldiers of the war of
1812.

The chairman stated that this resolu-
tion would, under an order already
adopted, go to the Committee on Reso-
lutions.

The Chair then asked if the Commit-
tee on Credentials were ready to report.
Pending the answer much amusement
was caused by the reading of a Telegram
from Reynolds Casey, of New York, in-
icating that tourists were ready to greet
the Democratic nominee.

being ready to report, Martin, of Dela-
ware, chairman of the
Committee on Permanent Organization,
then made report in accordance with
the action agreed on last night and sent
in the press report.

Martin, of Delaware, moved the
previous question on adoption of report,
but subsequently withdrew the motion.

It was moved that further action on
this report be postponed until the Com-
mittee on Credentials had reported.
Agreed to.

Committee on Credentials,
submitted his report. In the Massa-
chus, case it was unanimously recon-
mended to admit both of the contest-
ants, and that the two delegates united
cast the vote of the State. The sitting
members from Pennsylvania were re-
ported as entitled to their seats. There
was great cheering when the clause was
read declaring that the committee had
with singular unanimity decided in
favor of the sitting members and against
the admission of Tammany.

Carroll, of Kansas, asked to present
minority report and was allowed to do
so and to read the report himself.

The Minority Report.

signed by four members, declares that
the Democracy in the State of New York
is divided into two regularly organized
factions, both of which represent large
constituencies, which have held State
Conventions. The history of the coal-
ition between these two factions in 1870
is well known. And the opinion is expressed that no similar action this year
would result in the election of Demo-
cratic President as then. The minority
concludes with resolution declaring
that the Faulkner Convention delegates
have fifty votes in this Convention, and
that the Shakespeare Hall Democracy
have twenty votes.

with cheers and hisses.

port demanded the previous question and
a vote by States being asked, for the Cle-
rk called the roll.

the limit of debate, and the Chairman
announced that the fifteen minutes rule
of 1876 would be enforced.

would be sustained. The vote stood:
ayes 800, nays 100.

rules one hour would be given for de-
bate, forty minutes being allowed for de-
bate contestants and twenty minutes to the
committee.

Oxford borough was the scene of great
excitement on Wednesday last, caused by
the advent of John Harris, the Democratic
colored orator. Mr. Harris came into town
in the forenoon and soon the report spread
on the streets that he was to make a political
speech in the evening. The colored
men gathered in groups and consulted with
each other; prominent white Republicans
were called in council, and the conclusion
was that violence was to be employed to
prevent him from publicly expressing
his political opinions should he
attempt to do so. Open threats
of personal injury were made to him
if he did not immediately leave, and these
threats would have been carried into execution
early in the evening had not an intelligent colored citizen promptly inter-
ceded in his behalf. When the riotous feeling
had reached this height it was reported
from satisfactory source that Mr. Harris
had not come to make a speech, was not
going to speak and had left the town.
This ended the cries of tar and feathers,
hanging, etc., and the mob dispersed. It
is a shame and disgrace that many prominent,
influential and intelligent Republic-
ans of Oxford, the advocates of free speech,
free ballots and equal rights, give encouragement
to the lawless, mobbing spirit
that manifested itself on this occasion.


The Hancock and English club intends
holding a Democratic meeting in Oxford
hall, on Saturday evening next, the 28th
inst, and it is said Mr. Harris has been
invited to address the meeting. If this is
correct, the Republicans may again have
the opportunity of disgracing the great
principle of free speech which they pro-
fessedly uphold.

Rev. G. CAMPBELL, who is about to embark to the northwest coast of Africa as a missionary, under the auspices of the Presbyterian Church, was married recently in Monticello, Wright county, to Miss Louisa Kries, of that town.


Mr. CHARLES G. BROWN of the Fishers Landing Bulletin intends making the trip to St. Paul, a distance of about 1880 miles, by wagon roads, on bicycle, shortly, so saws the Bulletin. Rather rough road to travel in muddy time.


Mr. WEBSTER, living near Union lake, injured one of his legs few weeks ago, but paid no attention to it, and continued to work in the harvest field. Gangrene set in, and the leg will have to be amputated. His physicians think he cannot recover.


A NEW courthouse has been erected and finished in Monticello, Wright county, and now the matter is agitated of preparing the basement of the edifice to be used for Jail purposes. Wright county has no Jail, and its prisoners are now lodged in the Jail in Hennepin county.


NICHOLAS CROWLEY, ESQ., an old and much respected resident of our town, died of quinsy on Saturday morning last. Mr. Crowley came to Chatfield in 1856, pre-empted piece of land about three miles south of our village, where he has lived up to the time of his death. Chatfield Democrat.


Mr. JOHN A. AMUNDSON, of this city winner of the De Forest prize medal at Yale college, received the medal on Tuesday direct from the United States mint at Philadelphia. Its weight seven and half ounces, and being of gold is valued at 500. It is a neat medal and worthily bestowed. -Rochester Record and Union.


LAST Wednesday night lightning struck the house on Mr. Welsh Ashley's place, two miles north of town, and killed two horses belonging to Dan Cameron, who were engaged with threshing machine and had reached there the evening previous. The horses were piled one above the other and were evidently instantly killed, as both had hay in their mouths. Standardization Republic.


A STACK containing 50 unthreshed bushels of wheat was burned to the ground on the farm of H. H. Kinney, in the town of Lake, recently. The fire was started from some sparks blown from the steam threshing engine of Lee Sutton, which was being used on the place. The separator was also burned. It was with much difficulty that the barns and outbuildings could be saved. Lake City Leader.


DURING a thunder storm Wednesday morning, lightning struck stack of wheat on the farm of Mr. DEWITT, on Greenwood Prairie, burning that stack and another one standing nearby. Several stacks of wheat on the farm of Mr. Metcalf, near Elgin, were also burned by lightning during the same storm. On Wednesday night lightning struck three wheat stacks on the farm of H. H. Richardson, in Haverhill, and they were burned to the ground. Wabasha Herald, August 25.


AUGUST DELAER of Sibley county, a few miles from Le Sueur, sold his farm last spring and started for the Pacific coast with his family, seeking for better location. He visited California, Oregon and Washington Territory, and returned with his family on Thursday of last week, anxious to buy farm near the one he sold. He is satisfied after all his wanderings, that Minnesota offers better inducements to the industrious farmer than any other section of country he has seen. -Le Sueur Sentinel.


THERE is considerable loud and rather strong language used in this vicinity in regard to the lack of provision made for the support of the Connemara emigrants. These people are in destitute condition, no food and no work, and no prospects of either. A long and severe winter is before them, and they are but lily provided with clothes or shelter. Many of them are leaving and quite number are coming to this place, but there is very little that they can find to do in town of this size. -Morris (Sibley county) Tribune.


WHILE going home from Glencoe last Thursday night, Mr. George Hill, when within eighty rods of his house, was shot at by some one concealed in the grass by the side of the road. The ball passed through the frontispiece of his cap, and but for sudden movement of his horse, which brought his head out of its line, would have passed through his head. The would-be assassin, seeing that his first shot had failed, fired again, but fortunately with no better effect. The horse took fright and ran with his rider to the stable. It was close call, and the party who fired the shots meant to kill. Mr. Hill thinks he knows the party. -Glencoe Register.


LAST Sunday morning Mr. James McNamara and young Leisses went out southwest of the town to shoot prairie chicken, and when out of town some six or seven miles the former met with a severe accident. As he was placing his shotgun into the wagon the team started suddenly and caused its discharge. The whole charge of shot entered the fleshy part of his left arm, below the elbow joint, passing upward and onward through the arm, breaking one of the bones, and lodging in his shirt sleeve. Doctors Bigelow and Blood dressed the injured limb, and hope to save it, although it may be rendered useless. -Owatonna Review, Aug. 9.

or twice yearly, with a good coat of
lime wash. 1t prevents decay of the
wood, and adds greatly to the appear
ance of neatness and healthfulness. The
cellar too, under the dwelling house
should be thoroughly cleansed and aired
at this season of the year, and the walls
and ceiling well whitened. The lime is
great purifier and will keep the cellar
sweet and wholesome. A good wash
for cellars and outbuildings may be pre-
pared in the following way: Put half


bushel of lime into clean water-tight
barrel, and pour over it boiling water
enough to cover it four or five inches
deep, stirring it briskly until the lime
is thoroughly slaked. After the shaking
is completed add water gradually; stir
ring it well until thin enough to use.
Then add a pound of salt and two
pounds of sulphate of zinc. This will
cause the wash to harden well, and will
prevent its cracking or rubbing off.
Almost any desired shade of color may
be given it by the addition of different
inexpensive pigments. Yellow ochre
will give shades ranging from delicate
quantity employed. Lamp black pro-
duces shades from gray to lead color
A good stone color may be obtained
by adding two pounds lamp black and
four pounds raw umDer to the quantity
of wash made by the above receipt. For
out door work, a tTifie of color is an i'm
provement, as it is less glaring; but for
cellars, or the inside of hen houses, or
any other place where the wash is used
partly for its effect as a disinfectant,
the less there is added to the lime, water
and Sulphate of zinc, the better. 1t is
easily applied, as a few splashes here
and there, whether on the ground OF
the cellar bottom, viii do no harm; the
principal thing TO be remembered is to
keep the wash well stirred so as to Sc
cure uniformity of color.


For the ceilings of rooms and other
inside work, where something a little
finer is required, the prepared kalsom-
inc, Switch may be bought dry, and in
any desired color or shade, is the best
thing. 1t is not expensive, is easily
prepared and needs no more skill in
using than any other wash or paint. If
this cannot be procured a good white
wash may be made as follows: Take
half pound of best white glue and soak
it in cold water for ten or twelve hours;
then heat it carefully, without allowing
it to scorch, until thoroughly dissolved.
and stir into it fifteen pounds of Paris
white, adding hot water until it is thin
enough to use. The walls should be
thoroughly cleansed before apply ing the
wash, which must be allowed to cool
before using.-NetU England Farmer.

letter to a chum in his city home.

No doubt (he wrote) you imagine I am dwelling in a sort of rural Arcadia, and just as far as physical nature goes, I am, for there can be nothing more green than the hills, nothing more clear, cool or limpid, or musical than the brooks that everywhere ribbon the valleys. Paradise itself could not produce more life-giving breezes, and yet my life is a burden, because the girls—and they are greatly the majority of my pupils—are such wide-awake, mischief-loving, tormenting beauties as I've never before known to one person to manage. They will have their own way, and completely demoralize the school; they tease, coax and wheedle me out of my most important rules, and when endurance ceases to be a virtue, cast upon me such reproachful glances and put up such pouting, pretty lips, that a fellow is tempted to seize his hat and vanish to the ranch, as they say West. But in spite of my complaints, don't imagine me subjugated. I have at last issued positive commands for the students not to range out during study hours, as has been the practice.

A sort of Gypsy encampment is located near an isolated nook among the hills and of course the pretty heads of my female scholars are completely turned and have not only laid down the law against visiting the camp, but fixed penalty thereto.

Now I know you will raise your hands in holy horror when I tell you that after exhausting every other form of punishment, from the ounce cap to writing lengthy compositions (the bitter abhorrence of every feminine heart) and all to no purpose, I have in this instance, resorted to the old-fashioned one, the ferrule. And so help me fate, I will carry it to the bitter end, and make every little hand smart whose owner disobeys, or my name is not Paul Cheney.

The school house where our hero presided was situated some distance from the village where he boarded and the walk, though pleasant, was lonely and passing graveyard. And of late weird tales had been told of ghosts who walk there by moonlight, and in one or two instances when the school-master had been beating he had observed an object clothed in white flit at a distance before him, and in his very path. Though a trifle startled, he had no doubt that it was a riddle that time would unravel. Therefore, upon the night when he had remained writing to the city friend, as he hurried homeward to-be in time for supper, he gave the matter no thought, and had reached the boundary of the graveyard when he was confronted by the white-robed apparition, approaching him with extended arms.

The suggestions natural to its appearance were the reverse of pleasant, yet he never dreamed the ghastly visitant was other than earthly, and quickened his pace to meet it, but to his astonishment it disappeared as quickly and entirely as if swallowed by the earth. Not little startled and puzzled, he hastened home, but kept his own counsel.

The next morning he proceeded to school more early than usual and spent some time in accommodating the walk of the ghost, and evidently to his satisfaction, for the broad smile that illuminated his face as he entered the school-room appeared to assure the pupils that the teacher was in the best humor, and they would accordingly receive many inducements.

At recess a number of pretty heads were in close consultation, and Sue Salmon, black-eyed beauty, said with a pout:

"Wasn't it mean for Mr. Cheney to threaten to whip any one who went up to the gypsy encampment? Just as if he dared to do it!"

"I would like to see him ferrule my hand," chimed in May Ellis.

"Or mine, either!" exclaimed Kitty Dalton. "What's the use of being such cowardly ninnies, girls? Let's go in spite of him."

"I will pay for any girl who will go with me to-day to have her fortune told," laughed Sue Salmon, merrily.

"Will you? Then we will all go, even if I have to submit to the punishment," answered May.

It was decided to run the risk, and accordingly when school closed at noon they marched off bodily to learn the mystery of the future.

THE United States circuit court for the district of Maryland, upon a charge of interfering with supervisors of election and United States deputy marshals and who now petition this court for writ of habeas corpus and certiorari on the ground that the statutes under which they were indicted and tried generally known as the federal election laws, are unconstitutional and void.

This court, in a long opinion by Justice Bradley, holds: First—That the federal election laws are constitutional and valid. Second—That circuit courts have jurisdiction of indictments under these laws. Third—That under the constitution congress has supervisory power over the regulations made by the state for the management of congressional elections, and may either alter, modify or add to them, or make entirely new regulations. Fourth—That in the exercise of such supervisory powers congress may impose new duties on officers of election, or additional penalties for breach of duty, or provide for the attendance of officers to prevent fraud and see that elections are legally and fairly conducted. Fifth—That the exercise of such power can properly cause no cessation of regulations or jurisdiction, because the authority of congress over the subject is paramount and supersedes all inconsistent regulations of state. Sixth—That there is nothing in the relation of state and national sovereignties to preclude cooperation of both in the matter of elections of representatives. Seventh—That congress has power under the constitution to vest in the circuit courts appointment of supervisors of election. Eighth—That the provision which authorizes deputy marshals to keep the peace at elections, is not unconstitutional, and that the national government has the right to use physical force in any part of the United States to compel obedience to its laws. Ninth—That the supervising power of congress includes power to compel state officers of election to observe such state laws with regard to elections of representatives as congress may have left unchanged. The petitions for habeas corpus and certiorari are denied.

A similar decision was rendered in case of Augustus H. Clarke, an election judge of the city of Cincinnati, in which the question of the constitutionality of the federal election laws was also raised.

Justice Field dissented from the opinion of the court in both of the federal election law cases, and read a long opinion, in which he maintained that it is not competent for congress to punish a state officer for the manner in which he discharged the duties imposed upon him by state laws, as in the case of election Judge Clarke. The judicial power of the government, he argues, is limited by the constitution to cases in law and equity arising under the constitution and laws of the United States, and to certain other cases which the constitution enumerates. It cannot be enlarged by congress so as to embrace cases not enumerated by demonstration. Further more, the federal law to punish state officer for the manner in which he performs the duties imposed upon him by the state, asserts a power inconsistent with and destructive of the independence of the states in matters over which their authority has never been surrendered. If the federal government can punish violation of the laws of the state, it may also punish obedience to them, and trade punishment according to its own judgment of their propriety and wisdom. It may thus exercise supervision over legislation of the states subversive of all their reserved powers. If the federal government can do this, the fourteenth amendment in its inclusion, and the states may at any time be degraded to the level of municipal corporations, visiting at the will of congress. After some further remarks upon the character of the federal legislation since the war and its bearing on reserved rights of the states, Justice Field says: that until recent decisions in the Virginia cases, he could not have believed that the former carefully considered and regarded judgments of this court upon propositions of constitution and upon the general character and purposes of that instrument would be disregarded or overruled, but these decisions in the Virginia cases do in his judgment institute a new departure, and with no intending any disrespect to his associates, Justice Field is of the opinion that the rules laid down in these and the present cases, tend toward the subversion of our federal system into one consolidated and centralized government. Justice Clifford concurs in Mr. Field's opinion.

WHAT IS THOUGHT IN LONDON OF THE Laureate's Latest Work.

The St. James Theater was crowded by a fashionable audience, anxious to witness the new one-act play by the Laureate entitled "THE Falcon" and founded upon a well-known story in Boccaccio.

The tale, it may be noted, has done duty before on the stage, having been set to music by M. Gounod, under the title of "La Colombo," an English version of which was given some years ago at the Crystal Palace. Mr. Longfellow, too, founded one of his "Tales of Wayside Inn" upon it, and now Mr. Tennyson has dramatized it. The story, which is the ninth novel of the Fifth Day, is a simple one, and may be thus summarized from Boccaccio: A certain young Florentine, Federigo of Egli Albright, is in love with a lady called Madonna Giovanna, and, to gain her affections—we quote from the excellent translation edited by Mr. Wright, F. S. A.—used to be continually giving tilts, balls and such diversions, lavishing away his money in rich presents and everything that was extravagant.

Thus he ruins himself and retires to the country, where his only amusement and source of sustenance was hawking. The lady's husband dies, and she goes into retirement with her son. This lad meets Federigo, admires his pet hawk, and falling in, with a sick child's fancy, nothing would suit him but the Knight's much-prized hawk. Giovanna goes, although unwillingly, to beg it, and then the Knight who is very poor, at his wits' end to entertain her worthily, kills the bird to furnish a meal for her and her son. Thus, when the lady makes her request he cannot grant it, much to his sorrow, but she is so struck with his magnanimity that after her son's death, when she comes into much wealth, she marries him, and Federigo, we are told, "lived in all true happiness with her, and was better manager of his affairs for the time to come."

Such is Boccaccio's story, but Mr. Tennyson has considerably modified it. He opens in the poor cottage of the impoverished Knight, and we see his joy when he hears that the Lady Giovanna is in his neighborhood, while we learn also how dear his falcon is to him. The lady comes to the house, the falcon is served for her meal, as in the original, and then she prefers her request. We are told, however, beforehand that she has refused his love since her widowhood on account of an ancient feud between their houses, and that also makes the petition more difficult. Of course the Knight cannot grant it, and then the lady falls at his feet, conquered by this additional proof of his love, and they agree together to look after her sick son.

In all honesty, and with every respect for the Laureate, the little piece, though it is written with some neatness and point, shows but few traces of the poetic power we might reasonably expect. There is a vast amount of domestic detail, and the Knight's poverty is insisted upon in many speeches, which are intended to be humorous but which are rather dreary. Thus, for example, we find the serving pan, Filippo, who is sort of feeble Jaleb Balderstone, and who is evidently modelled on Shakespeare's clowns, coming to say in perplexity, "spoons, my lord," meaning that there are none in the place; and the old nurse whines about breaking the salad-bowl. Here and there we come across lines which will bear quotation. Thus, for example, Federigo tells the lady that she can "touch no chord" in him that would not "answer you in music." "It wore the lady's chaplet round my neck
It served me for blessed rosary"

Again, when she returns one of his gifts, some diamonds he had presented to her in old days, she says:

"No other heart
Of such magnificence of courtesy
Beats out of heaven"

But at the same time the language, though always happy, never seems to rise to the Tennysonian level; and indeed, the poet seems to have striven rather to be facetious than to be poetical, and with indifferent success. The piece is pretty fine, but it ought to have been something more, and it indubitably leaves sense of disappointment. It was well acted. Mr. Kendal gave due emphasis to the part of the Knight. article:
Death of This Pioneer Settler at Duluth.


The older residents of st. Paul were both
surprised and shocked yesterday to hear of
the death of Hon. Luke Marvin, of Duluth.
He had been sick for some little time, but
his critical condition was not understood
outside the family circle, and to most the in
formation of his sickness and death came
simultaneously.


Mr.. Marvin was born in Hinckley, Lei
cestershire, England, in 1920. In 1852 he
came to this county and thirty years ago set
tied in st. Paul. His enterprise and public
spirit soon attracted attention and he was
chosen member of the city council and
made its president. In 1861 he was appoint
ed register of the land Office at Duluth and
removed to that city, where he has since re-
sided. He was member of the legislature
for one term and subsequently appointed
postmaster, which position he occupied at
the time of his death.


MIR. Marvin was a man of great public
spirit, and always active and foremost in pro-
noting public interests. He was generous to
fault, and utterly unselfish in his devotion

Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.


APRIL 8, 1880.


Notwithstanding the unfavorable weather
which prevailed during the whole of
the day the cornerstone of the French
Memorial chapel was laid yesterday
afternoon in the presence of large
assemblage by Fredericksburg Lodge,
No. 4, of Masons, under the direction
of Grand Master Peyton S. Coles. The
parade and ceremonies were conducted in
drenching rain, but proceeded in due order,
and commanded the eager and respectful
attention of the multitude for an hour under
these uncomfortable circumstances. The
stone bears the following inscription:
"Laid April 8, A. L. 5380, A. D. 1880,
BY Fredericksburg Lodge, No. 4, A. F.
M. M., Wor. Peyton S. Coles, W. M.,
presiding"


A sealed box was deposited in the stone
containing mementoes, Masonic and public
records, copies of the FREDERICKSBURG
papers, the Richmond Dispatch, the New


building is to be of granite, and is of the
Gothic style of architecture modified. It is
presented by Mr. S. G. French, now of
New York, to the Presbyterian church as
memorial of his deceased daughter, Miss
Maggie P. French, and will be used prin-
cipally for the Sunday school. Its cost
will be nearly 100000.


A number of visiting Masons were
present, including some members of Culpeper
and Orange Lodges, the Rich-
mond Commanders of Knights Templar
and W. B. Isaacs, W. M. Drinkard, and S.
J. Quinn, of the Grand Lodge of Virginia.
The address of Judge Wexford was de-
livered in the courthouse. It was an elo-
quent and able production. The principal
topic was the triumph of the faith of the
Bible over false systems, as illustrated in
the decline of Islamism and the wonderful
growth of the American republic from the
settlements at Jamestown and Plymouth
Rock by men who brought the Bible with
them, which have spread until the cham-
pion of free, Christian commonwealth extends
across the continent. The address will be
published.


A supper was given to the visiting Masons
at the Exchange Hotel last night. The
Fredericksburg Commander acted as es-
cort to the Lodge during the ceremonies of
yesterday.


Intelligence was received here to-day of
the death of the venerable Lewis B. Will-
iams, of Orange. Mr. Williams died on
Wednesday, after an illness of about
a week. He was in his eightyeth year, and
it is said, had never known days sickness
until his last illness. He was Past Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of Virginia
and held the office of Commonwealth's at-
torney in Orange since 1864. He was re-
elected last year by large majority over an
active and vigorous opposition.


The state regatta, which is to take place
here July 9th, is attracting much interest.
Last week more than one hundred of our
principal business men joined the Kappa
Hammock Club as honorary members. It is
the intention to assign to the honorary
members charge of all the business details
attending the regatta, leaving the active
members of the Club free to devote them-
selves to training. The Rappahannock
will make most determined effort to win
back the prize cup.


Increased accommodation will be pro-
vided for visiting crews, and special ar-
rangements will be made for the entertain-
ment of members of the press, and also
whether it is agreed that the regatta shall be
a great success in all respects, leaving no
room for complaints, as was the case in
the first regatta on account of the entire
novelty of the thing and the unexpected
large proportions which it assumed.


The Odd-Fellows celebrated the sixty-
first anniversary of their order with a pa-
rade by candlelight and an address by Rev.
J. James Carmichael. This order has a
large and influential membership here, and
a flourishing condition.


A new society, called the Sons of Toll,
was organized here last week. Mr. Charles
L. Johnston, who instituted the popular
society of Sons of Sobriety, is at the head of
the new order. Temperance and benevolence
to members are the principal objects.
The Baptist church has presented its pas-
tor, Rev. Dr. Dunaway, ticket to the
Southern Baptist Convention.


The canvass for Municipal Offices pro-
ceeds quietly. There are rumors of dark
horse in reserve for the governorship, but no-
w these Captain J. W. Seper and ex-
Mayor X. Y. Berry are the only candidates.
A light during the supper at the hotel
was seen among some of the walkers
in the streets.

WASHINGTON. Sept. 15.—The work of taking the census of the Indians of the United States will be commenced on October 1st under the supervision of Major J. W. Powell, Director of the Bureau of Ethnology of the Smithsonian Institute, assisted by Col. Garrick Mallory, R. L. Packard, H. W. Henshaw, F. D. Himan and Clay Macauley. be had in this country, even by the

Branch.


John Mccullough played at Galveston last
week, and after his first night drew large
houses.


Pauline Markham has left her husband Gen.
Markham, and is now in Arizona looking for a
new one.


Ada Gray has drawn much money from the
pockets of the Michiganders during the past
two weeks.


Den Thompson will spend this week in a
tour through the land of steady habits and
wooden nutmegs.


Dickey Lingard and her company will spend
the week at Cleveland, and will present the
usual attractions.


Mary Anderson catered to the "culchaw" of
Boston last week to good purpose having had
overflowing houses.


Aldrich and Parsloe have done splendidly at
Chicago during the past week, and will stay
there six days longer.


Kate Claxton has been doing the Wolverines
during the past week, and has met with a
flying degree of success.


Ada Cavendish will open at Washington to-
morrow evening. The Congressmen have be-
gun to expectorate already.


"Dr. Clyde" has had a good run at Philadel-
phia, and finished last evening. Critics are
divided as to the merits of the play.
Mckee Rankin had to satisfy claim for
$255 at Cleveland last week before he was per-
mitted to appear in "The Danites."
Bartley Campbell's latest success, "Fair-
fax" was produced at the Novelty theater,
Brooklyn, last week, to large houses.
If Miss Dora Wiley is not the homeliest
woman on the American stage, the artists of
the Dramatic News ought to be crucified.


Bandmaun opens at Indianapolis tomorrow
evening. We had hoped that the Indiana
capital would be spared from public broils.
Fanny Davenport has done splendidly in Bal-
timore, appearing to good advantage in nearly
all the characters she habitually represents.
Manager Ford, of Washington, has started a
company on the road with "The Galley Slave,"
and it is now going over the Southern circuit.
Ella Wesner contemplates return to this
country, and will make a tour of the principal
cities, safe conduct being guaranteed by Tony
Pastor.


The Emma Abbott company received a severe
scoring from the New Orleans papers last week.
Their performances were pronounced beneath
criticism.


After a tour through Michigan this week,
Mckee Rankin and wife will open a two week
engagement at McVicker's theater, Chicago,
next Monday.


"The Milesian Thrush"—Alice Murray, who
was so popular here a few years ago, now
weighs 259 pounds. A pretty healthy thrush,
one would say.


Rice's Surprise Party did good business at
the Union Square theater, New York, for the
past two weeks. The company is an unusually
strong one in every respect.


Haverly's Juvenile "Pinafore" company cap-
tured the public of Louisville last week. The
theater wasn't large enough to accommodate
those who wanted to see the show.


Maggie Mitchell's season in Chicago has been
unusually successful. She will appear at the
Opera House here on Thursday evening next
and may be assured of a cordial welcome.
Adah Richmond has been obliged to cancel
all her engagements for the remainder of the
season on account of ill health. If she would
let booze alone, her health would no doubt
be better.


Frank Mayo is meeting the approval of the
public but the opposition of other managers
by reducing prices at the Olympic theater,
New York, of which he has lately assumed the
management.


Lena Tettenborn has made a hit in Katrina
Munchansen at New York. The play, "50
West" was a failure everywhere else, and so
was the actress, but there is great danger that
both will recover lost ground.
John Stetson, of Boston, has secured the right
to produce "The Pirates of Penzance" in New
England. He only paid $4,000 for the privi-
lege, and it is the opinion of everybody com-
petent to judge that he has made a good bar-
gain.


Mrs. Tony Pastor has projected a benefit for

husband. It will take place tomorrow even-
ing, and a jammed house is already assured.
Mrs. P. made all her arrangements without
consultation with anybody.
The Strakosch opera company have met
with but indifferent success during their Bos-
ton engagement. Miss Blanche Davenport
was prime favorite, but as she had abjured
her name she received some pretty rough
treatment from the newspapers.

find him myself. I will try." So slipping
her hat on her head, she went out
of the yard, and looked up and down
the street with all her blue eyes.

Now the street, which ran down to
the depot at one end, went straight up
to the end of the town to a hill at the
other, and then turning, ran over a high
railroad bridge which sprang from one
high cliff of the hill across to
the other side. Jessie could see not a
sign of Benny toward the depot; but up
the street, away up so far that it was
only by his scarlet sash that she
knew him, she could see Benny put
ting for the turn in the road as fast
as his fat little legs could carry him.
With bound and feeling of mortal
fear at her heart, Jessie sprang after
him. It seemed to her as if everything
happened in a minute. As she sped
along she could hear the latest passen-
ger train just putting into the depot be-
hind her—and, yes—there in the road
was one of Benny's little silk carriers,
but she could not stop to pick it up.
What if Benny should get to the bridge
just as the train came along, and tumble
off! He was liable to fall, anyway,
and the poor little chap knew so little
of treacherous bridges that he might
even run right off of his own accord.
On, on she ran, her cheeks like fire,
her hat flying off behind her, her fore
head covered with bright little drops!
But she thought nothing of herself. All
her mind, her heart, were in her feet,
and they were leaping after Benny!
He was now out of sight. She came to
the turn of the road, the bridge was be-
fore her—but Benny, where was he?
She could not see him, but oh! she
could hear him, screaming with fright
and calling, "Mamma, sister, some-
body! Do turn help little Benny! Oh!
oh—oh!"

Jessie could see down the track as
she ran to the side of the bridge. The
roaring train was coming along toward
her at a great speed. Where, oh! where
was Benny? Jessie gave a great cry.
There he was hung by his petticoat to
a great spike on the under edge of the
bridge! There he was, juggling and
struggling to get himself off—and
if he did! There were the shining rails
and the ing train that would crush him into
a horrible bleeding mass! All this
rushed through her mind while she was
acting. Laying herself flat out on the
bridge, with only her head and arms
over the edge, she said, gently, "Ben-
ny, keep still. Here is sister. Put
up your arms and take her hands."
The little fellow was usually obedient,
and he instantly did as he was bid.
When she had him closely clutched by
both hands Jessie began to have hope.
She said a little prayer in her heart. It
was this: "Dear Heavenly Father, give
me strength to hang on." That was
all, but she felt as if she would be able
to hang on a great while when she had
finished it. But what was this? The
train had come along more and more
slowly. It finally stopped. A man
jumped off and shouted, "Hold him,
hold him! I'll be there in a minute"—
and he began to climb the sides of the
great embankment as fast as ever man
could.

Benny by this time was sobbing, but
not struggling. The spike still held his
dress fast, so that his weight was not
fully depending from Jessie's arms.
She kept comforting and soothing him,
while she trembled and wept herself,
but still hung onto the little fat arms
with gentle but strong grip. Oh! it
seemed ages before that kind fireman
laid himself down flat beside her, and,
reaching carefully out, grasped the
clothing of the naughty runaway, and
finally set him safely on his feet. But
at last it was done, and before Jessie
could get her breath to say more than
"God bless you" he had sprang down
the rocks again, and was soon on the
engine steaming away!

Oh! what a time it made in the house
and the neighborhood when the whole
story was known! How proud and
glad mamma was of her brave and sen-
sible little daughter! How Benny him-
self began to understand his peril,
and promised never, never to run away
again. How papa hunted up the en-
gineer's assistant, and by his money and
influence made him conductor on the
road, and how that is, mean, Ben-
ny's very bright aunt—hugged first one
child and then the other, hardly know-
ing which she loved the most or was
the most delighted to have safe home
again! Jessie is a young lady now, and
I presume—being sixteen and very par-
ticular about her hair and the doings
of wearing train that she feels almost
too grand to remember what she loftily
calls the "goings of her childhood";
but Benny being only eleven, and still
in the Grammar School, resents the
least thing ever said against girls, and
especially against his sister. I have
known him to do what is called another
very naughty thing; and that is to
"pitch into" and beat a big bully who
said, "Huh! your sister's got awful big
feet and red arms!" And he answered,
while knocking the bully down, "Bood!"

Yesterday closed the eighth annual COM
mencement exercises of the University of
Minnesota. Like class day the attendance

always memorable one in every Academy
College or University in all countries where

graduate may come, his relations and friends

sire to be present to share in his honors, and
bid him God speed as he makes his parting
bow, and steps from the doors of his Alma
Mater out into the wide, wide world, to COM
menCe the battle of life for himself. Thus far
his antagonists have been books, and in this

sheepskin in his hand, he realizes for the first
time that for all time to come he must Ego it
alone" and fight his way through life single
handed.

University were crowded with carriages,

Yesterday closed the eighth annual commencement exercises of the University of Minnesota. Like class day the attendance of visitors was large. Commencement day is always a memorable one in every Academy, College or University in all countries where such institutions of learning exist. No matter from what part of the civilized world the graduate may come, his relations and friends all feel deep interest and an irresistible desire to be present to share in his honors, and bid him God speed as he makes his parting bow, and steps from the doors of his Alma Mater out into the wide, wide world, to commence the battle of life for himself. Thus far his antagonists have been books, and in this struggle he has had the assistance of kind and learned instructors, upon whom he leaned. But as he leaves the platform with his sheepskin in his hand, he realizes for the first time that for all time to come he must go it alone and fight his way through life single handed.

Yesterday morning broke clear and bright, and at an early hour the streets leading to the University were crowded with carriages, bearing visitors who were anxious to hear and see the interesting exercises. As before stated, the chapel of the University has seating capacity of some 800, but by packing the aisles and the large platform it will accommodate fully 1900. AND THE SUIT OCCASIONED THOROUGHLY

BEFORE MAGISTRATE VANDERGRIFT

An interesting case, involving the rights of customers of merchant Tailors, was tried before referees—Allen, Sissie, man, Wm. G. Woods and J. Wisler in Vandegrift's office, Wilmington.

The case was that of Isaac Taylor vs. John B. Triebler, merchant tailor; and the facts testified to by the plaintiff and his witnesses were about as follows: Taylor ordered coat and vest of cloth for $15, but on going for them at 10 s. this evening, May 5th, was informed they were not well done, but would be sent home that night, whereupon he had the money for them. He tried them next morning and found they would not fit, the coat being so small it would not button. On Monday he took the goods back and demanded his money, but Triebler refused to return it, though he offered to alter the coat, so that Tuesday evening Taylor again went to the store and tried on the coat, and although it felt better this time it proved misfit in other respects. Taylor declined to take the clothes, and asked Triebler to settle the transaction by returning him therefore the fifteen dollars paid. Triebler refused to return the money and then Taylor entered suit for the full amount with B. Pennington, Esq., as counsel.

The referees, after hearing the case, turned a verdict in favor of the plaintiff for the full amount of his claim and costs.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE NEWS AND COURIER: You say I had a week of sensation? You say, why not? What would a newspaper be nowadays that was not sensational? My letter to the News and Courier of the 18th of December from this city must have created sensation, judging from the editorials of the weekly press of the State, and the letters pro and con I have received from the State. And repeat what I said, or intended to say, that so of the South, who are held responsible by the American people for all the legislation of Congress, because we are in the majority in the Democratic party, and that party is in the majority in both Houses of Congress, are so manipulated by our Northern allies, though they are in the minority, that all our Federal legislation rebounds to the benefit of that section, and none, or almost none of it, to our benefit. Northern Democrats will vote with the Northern Republicans to defeat Southern measures. This has occurred repeatedly, and hence my aversion to the great Southern Democratic party continuing to play mammoth tail to the Northern Democratic pygmy kite.

and cooperate with the teacher in all things

an honest pride in the mental and moral cu-
lture of the young, in order to the elevation
of the standard of good citizenship.

time thought of for the Presidency, and
as a consequence it cannot be claimed
that the article was written to injure him
as a Presidential candidate. The Sun had
a series of articles devoted to THE
Scandals of Grantism, giving full and
unbiased account of the manner in
which Boss Shepherd plundered the District of Columbia. The Sun headed one
chapter of the first installment of this
history


THE STORY OF DE GOLYER GARFIELD,


And told it as follows;


In the spring of 1879 a lobbyist named
Chittenden came from Chicago to Washington to represent the firm of De Golyer
and Mcclellan, contractors. Chittenden appears to have known the ropes. He made
his approaches through Wm. S. Huntington, Cashier of the First National Bank, of
which Governor Cooke was President.
But the unforeseen happened: Huntington
died, and all of Chittenden's efforts went
for nothing. Instead of fulfilling the dead
Huntington's plans, the surviving members of the Ring attempted to defraud his
widow out of her property, and they might
have succeeded if she had not published
a suggestive letter from Hallett Killbourne to her husband, and hinted that
she had more in reserve.


But Huntington's death left Chittenden
in the lurch. He was about to return home,
when kindly fate led him into the presence
of Rev. Wm. Colvin Brown, who gently
intimated that his spiritual influence over
Governor Cooke was so great that he might
successfully exert it on behalf of a wooden
pavement, if properly rewarded. Chittenden told him to go ahead, and if he succeeded he should have $4,000. At Brown's suggestion Chittenden employed Richard
O. Parsons, a lobbyist, who, in the fall of
1879, was elected to Congress from Cuyahoga district of Ohio, but who, in the
spring of that year, was plying his trade.
Parsons' testimony: "I called upon General Garfield and gave him history of the case, and then stood, and asked him, as Congress
would adjourn in a few days, if he would
act for me in my absence and give the subject careful investigation. He at first
declined on the ground of pressing business but finally assented to have me send
the model, books, papers, etc., to his house
for examination. After a day or two I
called upon him, and he said he would prepare an opinion as to the merits of the patent, and attend to the case for me. I said
to him that I had a fee in the case of importance to me, and would be glad to
share it with him. The same day, or day
after, I left for Cleveland, and when I received my fee, some time after, from my
clients at Chicago, I deposited Gen. Garfield's fee to his credit in bank, and wrote
him."


Parsons further testified that he received
$1,000 at the time he was retained, and
subsequently got his contingent fee of
$4,000, making in all $5,000. Of this
sum Garfield received $500. But what
service did he render? He simply wrote a
paper and affixed his signature to it, recommending the Board of Public Works to
adopt the De Golyer pavement No. 2, together with the De Golyer and Mcclellan
process for ironizing the wood used in its
construction. That was enough. Chittenden immediately wrote to his clients:
"To-day and to-night's work has secured
the assistance of General Garfield. You
cannot overrate the importance of this concession. He is Chairman of the Committee on Appropriations, and holds the purse
strings of the National Treasury. Through
him must come every dollar of appropriations. I need not say that I now feel certain of success."


The books of De Golyer and Mcclellan
show that the first payment was made to
Parsons on the 1st of May, 1879. Garfield
was called into the case almost immediately. On the 18th of May, a new
application for the De Golyer pavement
was formally laid before the Board of Public Works, backed by Garfield. On the
20th of May, Garfield, Chairman of the Committee on Appropriations, reported an
item of $102,650.30, which the Board of
Public works had charged to the United
States. The charge was fraudulent. It
was based on false measurements and on
false assessments. But in advocating it,
Garfield said: "This Board have made
a full and accurate statement of the
expense of grading, paving and other work
done on the streets opposite such government property, and have forwarded to the
President of the United States a full statement of such expenses and an estimate of
the cost to the United States!"
